11. **Characters, second package: their lives.** "A living pool", with new characters arriving through doors where the routes from beyond the map come in, never appearing from nowhere ("Arrivals come through doors"; the doors are map data, with first-guess traffic until the edge markets exist), each newcomer's origin, reasons, name and backstory drawn as facts ("Who they are"), and heads rising where men lack one: a chief for a large crowd of loose men, a successor in a band, a leader for mutineers, and one among a fallen court's refugees ("A head rises where men lack one"), "Enough people, not enough good ones", "Hiring as a negotiation", quitting out of loyalty, which breaks the contract and is recorded, ongoing costs, and "Where characters keep their gold" (purse, hoard and their costs), and "Lending to kings" with debt tablets as evidence and claims, not entries in the score; and outlaws on the roads and seas: "Turning outlaw", "The way back" and "Pirates and bandits", which work the routes of item 7; and "Characters deal with each other", messages and in-person exchanges between characters in the same place; "The richest characters" extended to hoards; "Gold is a lifeline" in the kings' requests too, so every request that asks a king to give or keep gold says what that gold means to him; "Characters as sellers of news", free characters offering structured reports at a price they set; and the character requests rewritten after "Stakes, not dispositions", each character's starting system prompt giving him wealth as his victory and, from his traits, his strategy for winning it, the strategy chosen by formula and the prompt written once by a model from it ("How the strategy is made"), with a bold or a careful road from each character's appetite for risk ("Bold or careful, one goal"), script characters following the same strategy, with what gold, gifts, honesty and getting caught mean for him (item 4's report proposes the script's dispositions as persona habits: build this instead); reputation from losses abroad, characters who hear that a court loses its people abroad or puts others' to death growing wary of serving or visiting it, coded explicitly for script characters ("Jobs, not wages"); and, once outlaws exist, the Idrimi line in the primer ("Idrimi, the outlaw who became king" under Echoes from the archive). Also the pool's baseline, fees that clear the market, and characters working for themselves when service pays less ("A baseline, not a limit", "Fees clear the market" and "Working for oneself"), which replace the earlier rule that arrivals respond to demand; and loans and hiring between any two parties ("Lending to anyone", "Anyone can hire anyone"); and "Messengers are errands": from here on, a report or letter from abroad needs a carrier, someone hired, a traveller going that way, or the sender himself; and "Bands are a character's soldiers", bands drawn from the loose men of item 10+, with pirates as bands at sea ("Pirates are bands at sea"); natural losses without old age, and personas that describe experience, never an age ("No age in this game"); and the dead ranked below every living character in "The richest characters". Also the scoring change of 21 October 2026 ("Debts are facts; repayment is a choice"): strength and the richest characters count what is held, so the score stops subtracting back pay owed and the characters' ranking stops counting it, with the script kings' benchmarks recorded before and after.

    - **11e. Cities defended by their men, and a fair scoreboard** (added 29 October 2026, answering item 11d's review; next, before item 12's measurements, since it changes how games go and who wins). Item 11d found a city falling in the first season of every game (525 kingdoms fallen in 50 games, against 158 before), and the fragile city-states that survive winning 48 of 50 games against par. Haakon (29 October 2026): "didn't you say the millitary age male population will defend their city when someone storms, or? Is it still that easy to storm?", and "Agreed to all! Implement expertly!" Two causes, each fixed at its cause. First, the men of a city defend its walls. As built, "The people defend their land" counts only where no troop stands, only when an army enters a province, and as a resistance of 0, 1 or 2 whose thresholds (5,000 and 30,000 men) no city-state's men reach. A storm now meets the city's own men of fighting age on its walls beside any garrison, counted by their number as every unit is, as hostile as they are to the attacker, with the walls multiplying the defenders as they price the storm; the countryside's men still resist an army that enters the province, now by their number too rather than in steps ("The people defend their land" under War). So a small walled city is dear to storm and falls to blockade, hunger or a breach, and no capital falls in its first two seasons on most seeds, the builder rules' line for a playable game. The walls stay as the dossier gives them, with no floor invented; the numbers are first guesses, tuned in item 18. Second, each power is ranked against its own starting position. Par as a mean with falls counted as 0 let any survivor of a fragile position win. Instead each power's result is placed among the results its own starting position gets in the script games, a fall counted as the lowest, and the winner is the power whose result ranks highest among its own position's results ("One scoreboard for every power" under Victory). Then the final score blends that performance with the realm's size, both from 0 to 1, a first guess of equal weights tuned in item 18 so that every power has about the same chance of first place; every placement counts, so each king's and city-state's request gives the goal in words, to finish as high as it can, and the end and the reports show the score with size and performance beside it (decided 29 October 2026). Measured: at script play, wins spread evenly across the powers and across Great Kings and city-states, within noise, and the benchmarks recorded before and after. **Stop for review.**
    - **11c+. The map read at a glance, and the newest version at once** (added 29 October 2026; a lane beside 11e and item 12, since it touches only the web app's drawing and its offline cache). Haakon, on his phone after item 11c went live, first saw the old board, served by the offline cache, and then the true map with its names under the badges. To the design session's takes: "Other than that, I agree with all your takes! Make it be done expertly!" Four parts. Names give way to everything drawn over the land: a name is shown at a zoom step only where it touches no more important name and no badge, army or fleet counter, ship or envoy, its box measured from the rendered text rather than guessed from its letters (as built, `NameLevels` counts only other names, and the capitals' spaced small capitals run wider than its guess, so Babylon and Susa touch). Counters gather by zoom: below the step where a province's tokens fit beside its city, they show as one token per power in that province with its count, opening into the single tokens as the map is zoomed in ("Map on small screens"). A test fails if any shown name overlaps another name or a marker, at 390 pixels and on desktop, at every zoom step, from the opening and from a game in progress. And the newest version is the one played: a new version takes over at once on the start screen, and during a game a small note says a new one is ready and reloads into the same game when tapped, so a player is never shown an old build after an update without being told. Checked on a 390-pixel phone and on desktop, in light and dark mode, with pictures in the pull request.
